answer.label: Not the Dalai Lama — actually David W. Orr
answer.sourceLine: The Dalai Lama never said this. The words are a lightly paraphrased, truncated version of a passage by environmental educator David W. Orr, from his essay “What Is Education For?” first published in In Context no. 27 (Winter 1991). Orr’s original reads “…more ‘successful’ people. But it does desperately need more peacemakers, healers, restorers, storytellers, and lovers of every shape and form” — the viral quote swaps in “of all kinds” and drops his framing.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Adapted from Orr’s 1990 commencement address at Arkansas College

source.excerpt: The plain fact is that the planet does not need more ‘successful’ people. But it does desperately need more peacemakers, healers, restorers, storytellers, and lovers of every shape and form. It needs people who live well in their places. It needs people of moral courage willing to join the fight to make the world habitable and humane.
trail: Quote databases and social posts overwhelmingly pin this on the Dalai Lama (e.g. Goodreads’ Dalai Lama entry), but none cite a speech, book, or teaching of his.
The passage is actually David W. Orr’s, whose fuller original continues past the popular excerpt.
We confirmed the exact wording in the archived essay “What Is Education For?” at context.org (In Context no. 27, Winter 1991).
source.excerptNote: Orr’s original wording — note “of every shape and form,” which the viral Dalai Lama version replaces with “of all kinds.”

source.rightsNote: The source essay “What Is Education For?” was first published in In Context no. 27 in Winter 1991 (adapted from a 1990 address) and reprinted in Orr’s book Ecological Literacy (SUNY Press, 1992). As a post-1930 work by a living author, it is in copyright; rights rest with David W. Orr and his publishers.

author.metaLine: b. 1944 · American environmentalist & educator · Oberlin College
author.bio: David W. Orr (born 1944, Des Moines, Iowa) is an American environmentalist, author, and the Paul Sears Distinguished Professor of Environmental Studies and Politics Emeritus at Oberlin College. He is a pioneer of “ecological literacy” in higher education and the author of books including Ecological Literacy (1992) and Earth in Mind (1994). The famous “peacemakers, healers, restorers” passage comes from his 1990 college commencement address, later printed as the essay “What Is Education For?”

misattribution.heading: How it became a “Dalai Lama” quote
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook feel-good misattribution: a genuinely eloquent line by a working academic gets restyled and pinned on the Dalai Lama, where it spreads faster.

items.why: Endlessly credited to him on quote sites and social media, but no speech, book, or teaching of his contains it — as questioners have noted on Quora.

The circulating text drops Orr’s “The plain fact is that…”, removes the quotation marks around “successful,” and swaps his “of every shape and form” for “of all kinds” — a smoothed rewrite of the original.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is educator David W. Orr, in his essay “What Is Education For?” (In Context, Winter 1991).

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: Orr wrote the passage for a college commencement, as the payoff to an argument that education mismeasures itself by worldly “success.” His point is that a planet in ecological crisis needs people defined by care and repair — not résumé achievement. Stripped of that context and re-badged as Dalai Lama wisdom, the line reads as gentle spirituality rather than the pointed critique of modern education it originally was.
